note: mañana = tomorrow, la mañana = the morning. In Mexico people say “en la mañana” (in Spain “por la mañana”).

examples: Yesterday I went to the doctor.
What time does the movie start?
Today is a very nice day.
note: It ends in -a but is masculine: el día, buenos días.

examples: On Monday I start a new job.
note: Days of the week aren't capitalized. El lunes = on Monday, los lunes = on Mondays.

examples: What are you doing on the weekend?
I'll call you in the afternoon.
note: tarde = late, la tarde = the afternoon (until dark). In Mexico: en la tarde = in the afternoon.

examples: On Tuesday I have Spanish class.
On Thursday I'm going to the doctor.
On Saturdays I go to the market.
On Sunday we eat together as a family.
I'm going to Mexico next month.
This year I want to learn Spanish.
note: Mind the ñ: año = year; “ano” is a completely different (rude) word.
In Mexico: en la noche = in the evening, at night.

examples: I can't right now, I'm busy.

note: Typically Mexican. It means “right now”, in practice often “in a little while” or even “sometime later”.

examples: I always have breakfast at seven.
I never drink coffee at night.
After class we're going to the café.
I always have breakfast before work.
In January it's cold in the north.

note: In Mexico Mother's Day is always on May 10.

examples: In July we're going to the beach.
The weather is nice in October.
November 2 is the Day of the Dead.
In December there are a lot of posadas (pre-Christmas parties).
We arrived at three in the morning.
Sometimes I eat at the office.

note: Very Mexican: al rato = in a while, later (and sometimes much later).

examples: At Christmas we see the whole family.
note: Christmas Eve = Nochebuena; on December 24 families have dinner together.

examples: The church is from the sixteenth century.
At that time I lived in Puebla.
The deadline is up on Friday.
In the rainy season it rains almost every afternoon.
